method: Complete ordered editorial reading of Peri Tzadik, Lech Lecha 4–6: all 33 default canonical paragraphs in the three complete osiyos. For each paragraph, finite actually read candidates in both schools were compared with the actual argument and neighboring development. Complete target paragraphs were read; a whole target section was read whenever a reciprocal direction was approved. Previously published connections were reassessed against their unchanged context instead of duplicated. Positive and negative decisions are individual scholarly judgments, not scores, candidate-generator outcomes, or claims of exhaustive absence elsewhere in the library. Full paragraph and section hashes pin the text reviewed; they do not establish semantic relevance.

entries.assessment: The complete thirteen-paragraph ois was read in order. This opening presents the Midrash’s wine cases and the apparent exceptions, before the discourse distinguishes mitzvah wine, an attained future holiness, and a promise not yet actualized. The examined passages do not supply one uniform explanation for this introductory catalogue. The substantive explanations were placed beside the specific cases developed later in the ois; no extra connection was attached to this opening merely because it mentions wine.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Read in full. Its distinction between rightful desire for settled life and its proper time, followed by Isaac’s wine and future blessings, is useful for the developed Isaac argument at 4:6. It was approved at that precise later anchor, rather than presented here as an explanation of every exception in the Midrash’s list.

Approved. Torah hidden within the tefillin’s compartments explains a bond within worldly garments. The speaker’s recognition of Torah within his apparent expansiveness is retained, rather than reducing the relation to shared tefillin terminology.

The complete revelation remains future; a present foretaste is not described as its entirety.

Approved after the full paragraph was read. A day’s service becomes fixed in the heart and garments so that a new day’s service can begin. This directly explains entering his days as a developed condition of embodied conduct rather than a synonym for the original promise.

entries.assessment: The entire nine-paragraph ois was read in sequence. This opening sets out the Noah/vineyard Midrash and the Maharsha’s question about Adam, grapes, and who first drank wine. The actual spiritual mechanisms belong to the question and explanation that follow. Neither examined candidate resolves that initial textual-history dispute, so no separate link was attached to the opening catalogue.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Read in full. Noah’s planting as an attempted boundary against desire illuminates the motivation question at 5:2, where it was approved. It does not decide the Maharsha’s alternative readings about Adam’s earlier use of grapes.

Read with the complete five-paragraph section. The loss of restraint after leaving the ark explains Noah’s later failure but does not resolve the opening question about the history of wine from Adam to Noah. It was not presented as an answer to that separate problem.

entries.assessment: The full paragraph was read in the context of the ois’s later answer. It asks why Noah deliberately chose the vineyard after Adam’s failure. Kometz explicitly supplies a spiritual motive, which is enough for the forward comparison. Peer review removed the reverse connection: the displayed 5:2 quotation contains the question, while the reverse explanation depended on the answer at 5:8. No reverse was retained that a reader could not assess from the displayed source.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved in the forward direction after the complete one-paragraph section was read. Noah intended to restrain desire, yet a restraint without the right motive can fail. Not approved for the precise motivation question after the complete target section was read. It treats the failure of restraint after leaving the ark, but does not explain Noah’s deliberate inference that planting wine would perform a repair. entries.assessment: The whole paragraph was read, including the difference between Adam’s food and Noah’s, the quoted Zohar’s embodied inclination, the permission of meat, and the subsequent offering as atonement. The actual Zohar question is about the animal: the full witness says אי בר נש חטא בהמה מה חטאת. The new English therefore marks What sin had [the animal] committed? The primary passage is Zohar I 89b, also transcribed at https://www.zohar-stories.com/story/1.3.6. No canonical Hebrew was changed.

The relation of person and possessions gives content to flesh as atonement without suppressing the origin’s warning about further sin.

entries.assessment: The entire paragraph was read. It asks why the same human inclination first caused judgment and later became the plea for no further flood. Both approved comparisons explain this reversal, with one emphasizing the argument from the inclination at birth and the other Noah’s new capacity for restraint after the flood. Permission is not equated with the disappearance of temptation.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved after the complete paragraph was read. The inclination present from birth becomes a plea for mercy, clarifying the origin’s change in judgment. entries.assessment: The whole paragraph was read, including the greater number of sparks attributed to meat, Rav Chisda’s use of wealth, and the need for nourishment suited to Torah. Approved after all eighteen paragraphs of the target section were read. The animal can participate in human choice and exertion through being used as food. This provides a concrete direction for the additional animal vitality, and the reciprocal explanation was independently reviewed within the full target context.

entries.assessment: The entire paragraph was read. Meat eaten in holiness can straighten the heart; otherwise the same embodiment empowers the inclination and calls for blood as atonement. The chosen target specifies how both the food’s vitality and the eater’s desire are directed through Torah. An offering passage that does not explain this meal-and-risk mechanism was considered and rejected.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved after the complete paragraph was reread. Meat raised through Torah corresponds to the altar, with the food’s vitality and the eater’s desire both involved. This specifies what eating in holiness accomplishes and preserves the difference from merely satisfying desire.

entries.assessment: The complete paragraph was read. Its meat-and-wine claim is bounded by actual personal need for Torah, with wealth, ordinary diet, and borrowing distinguished. candidatesReviewed.reason: Approved after the complete long paragraph was read. Approved after the whole paragraph was read. What a soul needs can differ sharply from another person’s need; Rabbi Chanina’s own sufficiency coexists with concern for all Israel. This explains a personal allotment rather than imposing one quantity on every person.

entries.assessment: The whole paragraph was read as the answer to the vineyard question. The two existing parallels were reassessed and retained. The new Ishbitz passage adds a distinct danger: wine can create an appearance of completeness without the settled clarity required for service.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Existing independently reviewed reciprocal retained after the complete section was reconsidered. Suppression during the battle differs from use after a real victory. candidatesReviewed.ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 4

Approved after the full paragraph was read. Wine can make an incomplete person imagine completeness, whereas priestly service requires settled awareness. Its continued affirmation that created things should serve avodah preserves the distinction between misuse and a suitable use.

entries.assessment: The whole concluding paragraph was read. Noah cannot assume the bodily holiness that belongs to Israel’s Shabbat covenant and its partnership with God. The ending of the Ishbitz quotation includes the power for the following six days; it does not stop at an incomplete citation.

The inherited heading and bracket debris in the canonical opening were preserved; they were not used to invent a new source attribution.

Existing reciprocal retained after the complete paragraph was reread. A human can gain or lose, and the flags allow an acquired degree to remain while a new one is gained. It explains continuing motion without treating all movement as assured ascent.

The Rav target explains standing before the King through unification; the Ishbitz target supplies a sustained inward commitment rather than merely repeating the Tanchuma citation.

entries.assessment: The entire paragraph was read, including the creation-as-new wording and the five additional organs. entries.assessment: The whole paragraph was read together with the full ois and the timing argument of 4:12. Sod Yesharim’s strong future-perspective claim about suffering is translated directly and not softened into a different sentence; the explanation preserves the distinction between present hardship and its future disclosure.

Approved after the complete paragraph was read. Isaac sees the later growth within the act of sowing; present salvations draw from the comprehensive future salvation. It is not presented as a denial of the lived stages described by Peri Tzadik.

entries.assessment: The complete paragraph was read. The person works with the organs within his power and then receives divine completion in the five organs he cannot fully command. The existing Yisrael reciprocal was retained. The new Beit Yaakov quotation includes exertion within one’s power before the plea to the Craftsman, so the appeal does not authorize withholding the work.

candidatesReviewed.reason: Existing independently reviewed reciprocal retained after reassessment. Its accessible restraint and subsequent sanctification from above explain the difference between voluntary work and a condition a person cannot fully prevent.

entries.assessment: The entire paragraph was read, including the heart’s recognition, the instruction available through creatures, the animal ethical examples, and the blessing over bread. The Likkutei quotation uses its complete clear discussion of the inner spring, not the unreadable marker elsewhere in that full paragraph.
